Manual

Everything the FM-1 does under Tonitor. New here? Start with Playing it; to install, see Install.

Not a groovebox

No tempo, no steps, no patterns, no drum kit.

Tonitor is for sound heard for itself: texture, grain, movement and slow transformation. You play drones, gestures and textures, layer them, loop them freely out of time with one another, and shape them while they play. It suits acousmatic and electroacoustic work as much as live ambient music, dark ambient above all.

Playing it Generative paths Macros Latched keys The loopers The screen Scales Presets Sessions The granulator The reverb The engines FM — six operators, DX7 style ANIMA — a synthesizer played by a simulated hand CALIGULA — an organism

Playing it

ControlWhat it does
FX SEL ENV LFO EDIT GLO (top row)choose layer 1 2 3 4 5 6. The chosen layer's button is lit; the others glow while they sound.
PRESETS knobthe chosen layer's engine: FM, ANIMA or CALIGULA, left to right. Each layer keeps a sound of each engine, so turning back finds the sound it had.
HOMEa new sound for the chosen layer, on its engine (never the same family twice in a row). HOME lights for a moment.
OCT− / OCT+the chosen layer's octave, −3 to +3. OCT− is lit below the middle, OCT+ above.
the white keysplay the chosen layer in the scale chosen (ARP): the first white key is the root, each white key the next note of the scale, up across all 16. Voices come from one pool of twelve shared by all the layers: a note takes a free voice, so a layer has as many as its notes need — a chord on one, a single line on another — and a new note never cuts the release of the one before it while voices are free. With the twelve all busy, a new note takes the release that has rung longest (on any layer), else the oldest note held on its own layer, else the oldest held anywhere. (CALIGULA is one organism a layer, outside the pool.) A key lifted ends its note on the layer it was played on, so a held note keeps sounding while you choose and play another layer. The keys you hold on the chosen layer light up.
the rightmost black keySHIFT (lit while held; each press shows the audio's load in % of the time it has, now / at most since the last press, e.g. LOAD 62/91). Hold white keys and press SHIFT: they latch — they keep sounding after you let go, and their keys stay lit. Hold SHIFT and press a lit key to let go of it.
the two leftmost black keysthe chosen layer's generative path: the first AMBIENT, the second EXPERIMENTAL (lit while chosen; the screen says which). Pressing the lit one again goes back to OPEN. See below.
the black key before SHIFTEDIT, on and off (lit while on): KNOB 1–4 become four macros that shape the chosen layer's sound. See Macros.
the other black keysplay no notes (kept for other functions to come).
ARPthe SCALE page (ARP lit): SELECT chooses the root (C to B), ALGORITHM the scale. The root is shown very large, the scale under it; what you just turned flashes black on white. ARP again, or a layer button, goes back.
RECthe chosen layer's looper. Press to arm a new loop (REC flashes, the band shows ARMED and its number); the first note you play starts it (REC lights; REC and the number). Press REC again to end it: the loop is exactly as long as from that first note to this press, and it starts playing at once, round and round. Press REC again while it plays to overdub: the same again, a new loop over the others — up to 10 loops a layer.
REC held (1 s)empty the chosen layer's looper, all its loops: the whole screen flashes LOOP n / EMPTY.
PLAYpressed and let go: stop the chosen layer's loops, or play them again, each from its start. Held: the chosen layer's loops on the white keys, to bring each in or take it out (see The loopers). PLAY is lit while they play. SHIFT and PLAY, from any layer: if any loop plays, every loop on every layer stops (LOOPS OFF; the loops are kept); if none plays, every loop there is starts, all together from their starts (LOOPS ON). PLAY alone still starts or stops the chosen layer's own.
SELECT knobthe chosen layer's level: 1.5 dB a click, from OFF up to +4.5 dB. The message band says it as the knob's share of its turn, OFF and 4 % to 100 % (VOL 74 %); a layer starts at 87 % (0 dB).
KNOB 1the chosen layer's DJ filter: from the middle (off), left is a resonant low-pass coming down from 20 kHz to ~35 Hz, right a resonant high-pass going up from 16 Hz to ~12 kHz; the further from the middle, the more resonant. While you turn it, and for a second after, the whole screen is its dial (in the layer's colour, the mode and cutoff under it: LP 1.2 KHZ). Saved with the session.
KNOB 2the chosen layer's granulator: the middle is off (as it starts). Left towards dark ambient: long, overlapping, slowly drifting grains, pitched down now and then, darkened, fed back on themselves, sometimes frozen. Right towards scattering: short, fast grains, their timing, place, pitch and level jittered more and more, reversed, stuttered, full of holes, decimated at the far end. The further from the middle, the more grains and the less of the layer. While you turn it, the whole screen is its dial (DARK 40, SCATTER 25, OFF). Saved with the session.
KNOB 3the chosen layer's crush: the middle is off (as it starts). Left takes the bit depth down from 16 to 1.5 bits (the sound coarsens, then breaks up, quiet tails gating out); right takes the sample rate down from 44.1 kHz to ~300 Hz (metallic aliasing, then a stepped buzz). Both along curves that keep the first half of the way playable; the rate glides, it does not jump. While you turn it, the whole screen is its dial (BITS 6.5, RATE 2.6K). After the granulator, before the layer's limiter. Saved with the session.
KNOB 4the chosen layer's reverb send, 0–100 (40 at the start). While you turn it, the whole screen is its dial (SEND 40), as for the filter and the granulator.
SAVEthe SESSIONS page: PRESETS turns through the 64 slots (the number shown very large: red when the slot holds a session, faint grey with EMPTY under it when it does not; the session loaded says LOADED). SAVE on a saved slot loads it; on an empty slot it chooses it (the sound stays as it is) so the next save goes there. Either way back to playing. A layer button goes back without either.
SHIFT + SAVEthe chosen layer's engine's PRESETS page (see Presets); SHIFT + SAVE again, or a layer button, goes back.
SAVE held (0.8 s)save into the session loaded or chosen, at once; the whole screen flashes SAVED and the number. With none loaded or chosen yet (just after switching on), the first empty slot is offered: PRESETS chooses NO / YES, SAVE answers. On the SESSIONS page, SAVE held saves into the slot shown, whatever is loaded: an empty one asks SAVE NEW; one holding a session asks OVERWRITE? in red, on NO until PRESETS turns it to YES; SAVE answers.
SEQthe REVERB page (SEQ lit). There KNOB 1–4 are SIZE, DECAY, DAMP, MIX. SEQ again, or a layer button, goes back.
ALGORITHM knobthe chosen layer's pan, left to right in 41 steps. The message band says it (PAN L 50, PAN C). Layers start spread out: 1 and 2 half left and right, 3 and 4 a quarter, 5 and 6 near the middle.
USB MIDI innotes play the chosen layer, as the keys do.
MASTERthe level.

Generative paths

Each layer has a path that leans what HOME draws, on every engine. A path changes nothing already playing: it shapes the next sounds drawn on that layer. The path's key is lit while that layer is chosen.

PathKeyLeans towards
AMBIENT1st black keysounds for ambient, dark ambient above all: ethereal, melodic, often melancholic. FM draws drones, beating spectra (SPECTRE), the depths (ABYSS), bells, voices (CHOIR), bowed, hollow, blooming and tidal tones, never BRUIT, IMPACT, FRICTION, SHARDS or STATIC; then softer attacks, long tails, darker modulators, slow LFOs, no sirens, narrower glides, often an octave down. ANIMA draws mostly HAZE, GOLDEN, VOYAGE, TIDE, CHOIR and BOWL, never GRIT, SHARDS or MACHINE, with a darker tone, more space, a slower hand, long releases, no crusher. CALIGULA draws SPORE, VEIL and LITANY most, UNDERTOW, CARRION, MOTH, sometimes RUST; tuned on root, fifths, octaves, depths and unisons; slow swells, softer edges, fewer bursts and surges, a slower hand
EXPERIMENTAL2nd black keysounds for electroacoustic and acousmatic music: edgier, gnarlier. FM draws bruits, frictions, shards, static, impacts and iterations, brighter, bent more often (sometimes twice), never SPECTRE, CHOIR, BOWED or TIDE. ANIMA draws mostly GRIT, SWARM, SHARDS and MACHINE, never HAZE, TIDE or CHOIR, and makes them wild: the sliders near their tops (FM, grain, texture, density, a quick hand), the resonance often screaming, and on most designs a crushed sample rate, folding drive, a band of noise and scattered grains, all dragged about by the hand, often a fast tremolo tearing it apart, the comb ringing hard. CALIGULA draws WIRE, THORN, HIVE and RUST most, never VEIL or LITANY; semitone clusters and tritones; sharper, more driven, more bursts and surges, a quicker hand
OPENneither litevery family, kind and species alike, as before the paths. Every layer starts here

Sessions keep each layer's path, and the path each of its sounds was drawn on.

Macros

Press EDIT (the black key just left of SHIFT; lit while on) and the four knobs across the top stop being the filter, the granulator, the crush and the send: they become four macros that reshape the chosen layer's sound, while it plays, under a held note. Each is turned from the middle, which is the sound as HOME drew it; either way transforms it. While a knob turns, the whole screen is its dial, with the macro's name for this sound and how far it is turned (+40 %, -25 %, AS DRAWN). Press EDIT again to give the knobs back.

The macros are chosen for each engine, and for some by the kind of sound:

KNOB 1KNOB 2KNOB 3KNOB 4
FMBRIGHT: the modulation index, and the carriers tilted (the higher partials up)DETUNE (the carriers pulled apart: beating, chorus) — or SKEW for metallic and noisy families (every partial off its ratio: clangour)GRIT: feedback and saturation turning up; a low-pass, smoother, turning downMOTION: the LFO's depths; turning up, a tremolo, quicker and deeper
ANIMATONE: every filter up or downwhat the kind is about: GRAINS, AIR (the noise), FM (the index), VOWEL (the formant) or DRIVESPACE: the resonator wetter and ringing longer (brought in if the sound had none), or drierMOTION: the hand's pace, its LFOs and the tremolo
CALIGULAEDGE: triangles to squaresDEPTH: how deeply the pairs modulate each otherCHAOS (total feedback and drive) — or ECHO (the delay) for SPORE, VEIL, LITANY and MOTHHAND: how busy the hand is, its touches and bursts — or PULSE (the gates' speed) for HIVE, MOTH and WIRE

Each layer keeps the macros of each of its three sounds. HOME draws a new sound as it comes (its macros in the middle). Sessions and presets keep the macros with the sound.

Latched keys

Hold one or more white keys and press SHIFT (the rightmost black key): they latch, sounding on after you let go, and they stay lit. A key pressed while SHIFT is already held plays as usual (unless it is lit). Latches belong to the layer they were made on: the keys are lit while that layer is chosen, and on another layer the same keys play as usual, so a drone can be left on one layer while you play another. Pressing a latched key without SHIFT does nothing (it sounds already); SHIFT and the lit key lets go of it, and its note ends as a lifted key's would. Loading a session lets go of every latch. Latched notes hold voices of the shared pool: with all twelve busy, a new note can take one, even a latched one's.

The loopers

Every layer has its own looper of up to ten loops, and they are all free: no tempo, no grid, no quantising — not even between a layer's own loops. Each overdub is a loop of its own, as long as you made it (from its first note to REC), going round in its own length over the others, so they drift in and out of phase. Each plays back exactly what was played, to 0.73 ms. The keys go on playing the layer over its loops, and the loops' notes and the keys' never cut each other's notes off — but all of them share the pool's twelve voices with the other layers, so many loops and layers at once take voices from each other. A layer's loops hold about 1000 notes between them; nothing is lost when the FM-1 is switched off if the session is saved.

Bringing loops in and out. Hold PLAY (it does not start or stop anything held): the chosen layer's loops appear on the white keys, the first loop — the foundation — on the leftmost, each overdub on the next, up to ten, lit while they play; the screen shows them too (in the layer's colour: in; a grey frame: out). Press a key to take its loop out — its notes stop, the others go on — or to bring it back in: it comes in at once, from its start. With the loops stopped it chooses which will play: take out all but one, let go of PLAY, press PLAY, and only that one starts; then bring the others in, one by one, as the piece unfolds. Every loop is in when recorded. Sessions keep which loops are out.

The screen

From top to bottom: the layer number (very large, in the layer's colour), its engine (FM or ANIMA, in white), the family of its sound (in the layer's colour). When something changes (NEW, OCT +1, LOOP), a black-on-white message replaces the family for a moment. While the chosen layer's looper is armed the band below the engine flashes ARMED in red; while it records it shows REC, white on red. A message too long for the band at its usual size (EXPERIMENTAL) is drawn a size smaller. Under it, across the screen, the layer's level meter: a bar filling from the left with the layer's colour as it sounds (-48 to +6 dB), and a white mark at the level the SELECT knob sets (red at the left when the layer is off). At the very bottom, the layer's pan: a block in its colour on a track from left to right, with a tick at the middle.

KNOB 1 to 4 (filter, granulator, crush, reverb send) each show, while they turn and for a second after, the same full-screen dial: the knob's name and the layer, an arc from 7 to 5 o'clock lit in the layer's colour, a white pointer, and in large type what it does.

The REVERB page shows the title and its four values in rows, each with a bar; the row you just turned is drawn black on white for a moment.

Scales

One scale and root for the whole keyboard (and saved with the session); C major at the start. The root sits on the first white key, in the octave from C3 to B3 (each layer's OCT moves it); the scale climbs from there across the 16 white keys, so a pentatonic scale spans more than three octaves.

ScaleSteps
MAJOR0 2 4 5 7 9 11
MINOR NATURAL0 2 3 5 7 8 10
MINOR HARMONIC0 2 3 5 7 8 11
MINOR MELODIC0 2 3 5 7 9 11
DORIAN0 2 3 5 7 9 10
MINOR PENTA0 3 5 7 10
WHOLE TONE0 2 4 6 8 10
ENIGMATIC0 1 4 6 8 10 11
JAPANESE IN0 1 5 7 8 — the in (miyako-bushi) scale of the koto and shakuhachi, known for its sorrow

USB MIDI notes are not quantised.

Presets

Each engine has 64 presets, P1 to P64, for the sounds you want to keep and bring back on any layer. Hold SHIFT and press SAVE: the PRESETS page of the chosen layer's engine opens, four slots a page. PRESETS turns through them; a slot holding a sound shows its number in red and the sound's name, an empty one EMPTY in grey.

  • SAVE held saves the layer's sound into the slot chosen. Over a sound already there it asks OVERWRITE? first, on NO until PRESETS turns it to YES; SAVE answers.
  • SAVE loads the slot chosen into the layer (which crossfades to it, as to a new sound) and goes back to playing.

A preset keeps what draws the sound again, exactly — its seed, its path and the generation of the generators that drew it — and its level: all 192 take one sector of flash, beside the sessions. Saving erases flash, which silences the audio for a moment, as a session save does.

Sessions

The FM-1 always starts with no session loaded. There are 64 slots, numbered 1–64.

A session stores in full the sound of the engine each layer is on, and the other two as the seed that made them and their level (the same sounds, drawn again at once), so a session usually takes one 4 KB sector of flash. A session is the whole machine: every layer's engine and its three sounds, its path, octave, level, pan, reverb send, filter, granulator, crush and loops (playing or stopped); the scale and root, the reverb, and the layer chosen. They are kept in the FM-1's flash, in the area SLOOP uses for its projects (saving overwrites any SLOOP projects, presets and samples left on the device): dozens of typical sessions, at least ten even with six full loops. A session also keeps the seeds its sounds were made from, with the path and the generation of the generators that drew them: every generation is kept exactly as it was (a test checks thousands of sounds of each), so sessions and presets saved under an older Tonitor load with the same sounds after an update that brings new generators. Erasing flash silences the audio for a moment: a save uses blank flash when there is some, and the FM-1 blanks free flash by itself while nothing sounds.

The granulator

Each layer keeps the last half second of its own sound (at 22 kHz, 8-bit mu-law: a little grit is part of it) and plays grains out of it, after its filter. Each layer's granulator has a character of its own, drawn at random when the FM-1 starts and every time a session is loaded: the intervals its grains are pitched to, how often they reverse, stutter, drop out or freeze, the shape of its scattered grains, how far its feedback and darkening go, how it drifts. The knob's position is saved with the session; the character is drawn anew. When the layer's notes end, its grains ring on for about two seconds.

The reverb

A plate after Jon Dattorro (1997): predelay, input diffusion, and a figure-of-eight tank whose two allpasses sweep slowly out of step, so the tail stays in motion and never rings. Each layer sends to it after its level; the reverb's return is added to the mix before the master.

at the start
SIZEthe room: every delay 0.5–1.25 times Dattorro's (turning it bends the tail, gently)70
DECAYthe time to fall 60 dB, 0.4 s to about 25 s, whatever the size65 (about 3.5 s)
DAMPhow fast the highs die in the tail40
MIXthe reverb's return level, ×0 to ×450 (×1)

Layer colours: 1 yellow, 2 cyan, 3 pink, 4 green, 5 orange, 6 lilac.

The engines

FM — six operators, DX7 style

The classic six-operator FM (msfa, the core of Dexed: 32 algorithms, rate/level envelopes, ratio or fixed frequencies, feedback, LFO, pitch envelope). HOME draws a patch from one of seventeen families of sound objects (since 0.22 with their operators on the ratios they were designed with — before, a slip in the generator put nearly every ratio near an even multiple and the patches two octaves above the key; sounds saved then come back as they were):

FamilyAfter
METALbells and gongs: many carriers on inharmonic ratios, the high partials dying first
DRONEspectral drones: near-harmonic pairs detuned to beat, an index wandering over minutes
BRUITnoises: feedback and high ratios scattered by a sample-and-hold LFO
IMPACTstruck bodies, the pitch falling, the modulators dying before the carriers
ITERATIFiterative objects: a sound pulsed by its own LFO, square or random
GLISSEglissandi: a pitch envelope travelling octaves, slowly
SPECTREa spectral arpeggio: rich tones a few cents apart whose beating lifts one harmonic after another
ABYSSsub-bass rumble folded by feedback, breathing slowly
FRICTIONcreaking: sub-audio fixed-frequency modulators and random pitch
CHOIRvowels: carriers on the harmonics nearest two formants, a late vibrato
BOWEDa bowed string: a saw from feedback, the bow's pressure rising with the swell
HOLLOWodd harmonics only: a dark pipe
BLOOMa tone that opens over seconds and half closes again
TIDEthree stacks crossfading, one fading as the next swells, under a slow tide of level
SHARDSa tone broken by random steps of pitch and chopped by a square
STATICring-modulated bands from modulators nailed to audio frequencies
WINDbreath and gusts over a soft drone

Each patch is then shaped with care: modulators on high ratios turned down (their sidebands alias and scream), the brightness scaled down the keyboard so high notes are not shrill nor low ones muddy, rate scaling on the carriers. HOME draws several patches, measures each, and keeps one whose brightness suits the layer's path (darker on AMBIENT, brighter on EXPERIMENTAL) and that is not of the family the layer had.

About half the patches are then bent once more, gently (an operator detuned to beat, an envelope turned over to grow as it holds, the LFO waiting and then moving the timbre, an octave down, more feedback, a modulator's ratio moved to a neighbour, a partial nailed to a frequency). Every patch is rendered offline as it is made and given the gain that brings it to one loudness.

ANIMA — a synthesizer played by a simulated hand

A fixed-point port of the anima opcode from Vascular, rebuilt for the FM-1. While a key is held, a simulated finger rests on a virtual surface and drags one figure after another — orbits, figures of eight, scribbles, slow glides, now and then a flick — pressing in slow swells, and now and then lifting to land elsewhere. A ghost finger comes and goes on an irregular clock. Where the finger is, how hard it presses, how fast it moves and how long it has been down move the timbre, never the pitch.

The voice: two wavetable oscillators (24 band-limited single cycles), an FM pair, a stack of copies, a grain cloud, a filtered noise, a resonant filter, a wavetable tremolo; then the hand's chain: a downsampler, a waveshaper, a phaser, a second filter and a comb resonator tuned to the note. Each new sound is a design: which of these are in, on which waveforms, and for every parameter which gesture moves it, over what range, along what curve, plus a mod matrix of three to seven routes and Anima's eight sliders, drawn — often far from their middle. Fourteen kinds: HAZE, VOYAGE, GLASS, BELLS, GOLDEN (Anima's own) and BREATH, GRIT, SWARM, TIDE (waves of noise over a low drone), CHOIR (vowels, a formant the hand moves), SHARDS (glass grains scattered and crushed), BOWL (a beating inharmonic hum in a ringing comb), DUST (sparse crackle over a dark drone), MACHINE (a pulsing, folded mechanism). The filter follows the keyboard, so low notes are not muffled nor high ones shrill; the second oscillator's interval suits the path (consonant on AMBIENT, anything on EXPERIMENTAL); and an AMBIENT sound nearly always has a resonant space to ring in.

In Vascular a design plays up to six fingers, each a voice; here a layer has one voice, so the hand has one finger on the sound.

CALIGULA — an organism

The third engine, after the architecture of SOMA's LYRA-8 as Mike Moreno's LIRA-8 emulates it (BSD licence), rebuilt for the FM-1 and bent towards dark, restless textures. Eight oscillators in four pairs on two sides; each a triangle that its pair's SHARP pushes towards a square; each with a sensor and an envelope, slow (a long swell, a longer fall) or fast; each pair frequency-modulated at audio rate by its partner, the other pair of its side, a pair of the other side or the total feedback (the whole organism, saturated, fed back in). A hyper LFO of two LFOs (alone, AND, OR, XOR) opens and closes the modulation and gates chosen pairs into irregular rhythms; a short modulated delay (two lines, ~35 ms) choruses, flanges or warps it; a drive.

A CALIGULA layer is played like the others: the white keys play the scale's notes, and it is silent until a key is down. A key wakes the organism at that note; a second key on top moves the whole organism to the new note at once (a snap, not a glide), and letting go of it goes back to the key still held; letting go of the last key lifts the hand and the organism rings out. It is rooted: tuned around the note played, in intervals of it (octaves, fifths, unisons and semitone clusters that beat, tritones, the depths). The hyper LFO moves timbre, never pitch: no sirens.

Nobody touches the eight plates: a simulated hand does, while a key is held. Each species has its own hand: how often it touches, how long a finger stays, how many fingers at most, its favourite plates, quick taps against long holds. The first finger stays down until the key is let go, so the sound never drops out under a held key. Around the hand the organism has a life of its own: the modulation depths and the sharpness wander, oscillators fire in bursts at irregular times, and now and then the feedback and the drive surge for a moment. A pair's envelope may be slow: a swell of seconds, a release of up to nine seconds after the key is let go.

The hand often has a phrase: two to four plates it keeps coming back to, varied now and then, often on a pulse of its own (long, short, short, longer) — so it plays like someone rather than like chance. A pair the hyper LFO's gates never close stays under it all. HOME draws a new organism from ten species, tuned on one of ten sets of intervals (pillars of octaves and fifths, semitone clusters, the depths, the harmonics, unisons, tritones, fourths, a minor seventh, open fifths, a quarter-tone cluster):

Species
SPOREslow swells, held drones, breathing; low
THORNsharp, deep FM, driven, bursting often
HIVEthe hyper LFO quick and gating: irregular rhythms, bursts
CARRIONthe depths, heavy total feedback, the delay warped by the voices, surges
VEILmostly triangles, light modulation: the calmest
RUSTdriven, cross-modulated, surging, sometimes rhythmic
LITANYa slow choir: unisons and octaves beating, nothing sharp, a hand that stays
UNDERTOWdeep: heavy feedback and a warped delay pulling it under, slow surges
WIREhigh and sharp, clusters and quarter tones, a quick hand tapping, bursts
MOTHsoft triangles fluttering through the gates, on a pulse
